recap-2026-07.titulo: July's procedural pivot: AI enters courts, classrooms and Congress
recap-2026-07.subtitulo: The Dorantes package brings AI into 14 procedural laws, the PRI publishes its Ley General (General Law), and the SEP opens the school debate with UNESCO. (Edition as of the July 30 cutoff.)
recap-2026-07.contenido:
July 2026 was the most legislative month in the history of the issue. On July 8, Senator Agustín Dorantes introduced a package of 14 bills (iniciativas) that insert the same chapter — "Del uso de herramientas de inteligencia artificial" (On the Use of Artificial Intelligence Tools) — into the country's procedural laws: amparo (constitutional relief), criminal, labor, agrarian, commercial, administrative, electoral and military, anchored in a reform to Article 17 of the Constitution. The package's logic mirrors what the Judiciary had already set by precedent: AI as an auxiliary tool, with human oversight, not a substitute for the judge's reasoning.

A day later, the Ley General para la Regulación y Uso Ético de la Inteligencia Artificial (General Law for the Regulation and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence, PRI) was published in the Gaceta (Gazette): it proposes a Agencia Nacional de Supervisión de la IA (National AI Oversight Agency), a Registro Nacional de Sistemas de Alto Riesgo (National Registry of High-Risk Systems), and explicit prohibitions (behavioral manipulation, mass surveillance without a court order, social scoring, fraudulent deepfakes).

The Executive branch moved on two fronts. On July 1, SECIHTI presented Congress with its 13 technological sovereignty projects — Olinia, Coatlicue and the sovereign language model among them — including a proposed regulatory framework. And on July 20, the SEP presented, together with UNESCO, the framework for the national debate on technology, devices and networks in schools: 8 out of 10 students already use generative AI, and the government announced an initiative to the Congreso de la Unión (Union Congress) plus regional forums in August and September.

Academia also formally entered the picture: the Consejo Coordinador de Inteligencia Artificial de la UNAM (CCOIA, UNAM's AI Coordinating Council) was documented, created by rector's agreement and installed in May, with Pablo Pruneda Gross as coordinador (coordinator) — the AI governance body of the country's largest public university.

Methodological note: this edition closes as of the July 30 cutoff; if the month brings further developments, it will be updated.

recap-2026-06.titulo: June of the antechamber: regulation pushed to after the World Cup
recap-2026-06.subtitulo: The Executive postpones the regulatory debate until after the World Cup while Coatlicue misses its first deadline and service-facing AI consolidates mass adoption.
recap-2026-06.contenido:
June 2026 was the month regulation of AI got a date — for later. On June 30, from the morning press conference (mañanera), the Presidency announced that the national debate to regulate artificial intelligence and social media will begin once the World Cup is over: an explicit commitment to a broad discussion — authorities, experts and citizens — but also a formal postponement of an issue Congress has spent months pushing on its own.

Meanwhile, infrastructure racked up its first measurable missed deadline: the promised start date for construction of the Coatlicue supercomputer in Zacatenco (June 1) came and went with no groundbreaking. The project remains in development with a 2028 horizon and a reaffirmed investment of 6 billion pesos, but the specific promise of a construction start date went unmet — the observatory logs it separately from the broader project, as a distinct commitment.

By contrast, service-facing AI showed real traction: the ATDT's 24/7 Ventanilla (window/helpdesk) — which passed one million interactions since April — received national coverage in June documenting its continued use and operation. It is, so far, the government AI deployment with the strongest evidence of adoption.

On the legislative front, June closed with the introduction of the Ley General para la Regulación y Uso Ético de la Inteligencia Artificial (General Law for the Regulation and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence) (PRI, June 27): it proposes a national AI oversight agency (Agencia Nacional de Supervisión de la IA) and a registry of high-risk systems, and was expected to be published in the Gaceta (parliamentary gazette) in early July. The full floor debate will come after the World Cup; the pieces are already on the table.

recap-2026-05.titulo: May of the decree: AI reaches the DOF and the Senate accelerates
recap-2026-05.subtitulo: For the first time an AI reform takes effect in Mexico via the DOF (Diario Oficial de la Federación, Official Gazette). Meanwhile, the National Laboratory remains a pending promise.
recap-2026-05.contenido:
May 2026 marked a turning point for AI regulation in Mexico. On May 14, for the first time in history, a substantive AI reform took effect: the decree published in the DOF (Diario Oficial de la Federación, Official Gazette) amends the Ley Federal del Trabajo (LFT, Federal Labor Law) and the Ley Federal del Derecho de Autor (LFDA, Federal Copyright Law) to protect artists and performers against AI voice and image cloning without consent. The reform requires labor contracts to stipulate compensation for the use of AI-processed voice/image, and bans impersonation that induces error or replaces professional services, with penalties of up to 40,000 days' minimum wage. Before May, the only formal precedent was the INE's Institutional AI Governance Program (Aug. 20, 2025), but that applied only to the INE as an autonomous body.

On the legislative front, the Senate accelerated its Ley General de IA (General AI Law) initiative. On April 30, the committee chaired by Rolando Rodrigo Zapata Bello (PRI) confirmed that the multiparty proposal is "prepared for introduction soon," featuring a national AI authority, mandatory registration of high-risk systems, and a certification regime. On May 7, two more initiatives were added in the Senate: an LFT reform to regulate AI in the workplace, and the "forthcoming Ley General para Regular y Fomentar el Uso de la IA" (General Law to Regulate and Foster the Use of AI).

The executive branch announced two major infrastructure projects this month. On May 5, Sheinbaum unveiled Mexico's first "AI Factory," featuring the most powerful supercomputer in Latin America (with no public timeline for operation). On May 26, the ATDT opened the second call for applications to the Public AI Training Center, offering 30,000 free spots, running from May 26 to July 5. But the National AI Laboratory, originally announced for October 2025, still has no confirmed launch as of month's end. The Ventanilla 24/7 (the federal government's AI-powered virtual assistant) did confirm real-world operation, surpassing 1 million queries handled in 4 months according to the ATDT, which formally moved it from the "promised" category to "operating."

Private investment: on April 16, Flex officially announced $1 billion for hardware manufacturing geared toward data centers and AI in Mexico (Jalisco, Chihuahua, Aguascalientes), with execution in 2026-2028 and 5,000+ jobs. Google confirmed on April 20 that its first AI lab in Mexico will be located in San José Chiapa, Puebla, and has begun the bidding process.

PoPMa3HQQa0cG5dp4vQi.subtitulo: Federal government makes no new AI announcements as states take the initiative
PoPMa3HQQa0cG5dp4vQi.contenido:
April 2026 passed without visible activity on the federal AI tracker. The Mexican government held its implementation pace steady: 16 projects operating, 12 in development, and 17 promised, with only one unmet. A compliance rate of 84.7% that, nonetheless, reflects more inertia than progress.

While the federal level stayed still, states moved forward. The Congress of the State of Mexico (Estado de Mexico) built an initiative to regulate AI in the public sector, focused on ethical use and administrative procedures. Mexico City (CDMX) installed its "Digital Rights and Artificial Intelligence" working group, exploring applications in water management, public safety, and pothole repair.

The contradiction is plain: at least 14 federal agencies already use AI in sensitive areas such as oversight and security, but operate without a specific regulatory framework. The Chapultepec Principles, unveiled in January, carry no binding force. Only Banxico (Mexico's central bank) reports formal guidelines for AI use.

In Congress, the 138 legislative initiatives (iniciativas) remained static: 56 active, 5 approved, 59 rejected. No movement in April. The 17 court cases likewise saw no change. The legal landscape remains fragmented while technological adoption advances unsupervised.

MJsU17WZPYX5MqdWN27u.titulo: Marching without a compass: the month of broken promises
MJsU17WZPYX5MqdWN27u.subtitulo: March 2026: scattered legislative activism while operational projects stall
MJsU17WZPYX5MqdWN27u.contenido:
March 2026 marked a worrying turning point for government artificial intelligence in Mexico. For the first time since tracking began, the tracker registered a broken promise: the IdentIA forensic software and RAG system from LAB-CO, promised for February, never made it past the experimental phase.

While concrete projects stalled, Congress showed unprecedented legislative activity. At least five constitutional reform initiatives on AI were introduced during the month, including proposals from deputy Eduardo Gaona (Movimiento Ciudadano), Santiago González Soto (PT), and senator Michel González (PAN). All seek to empower the federal Congress to legislate on artificial intelligence, but none has advanced beyond committee.

The contrast is telling: in February, two significant promises were fulfilled with the AI regulations on dubbing and political campaigns. In March, zero operational progress, while legislative initiatives piled up competing with each other with no apparent coordination.

On the academic front, the Senate presented on March 11 the book "Inteligencia Artificial: hacia una nueva era en la historia de la humanidad" (Artificial Intelligence: Toward a New Era in Human History), where lawmakers agreed on the urgency of a National AI Strategy. Paradoxically, this declaration came the same month the government's first AI project failed to meet its deadlines.

The government keeps 42% of its announcements operational (16 of 38), but the trend is deteriorating. With one project now broken and multiple fragmented legislative initiatives, March exposed the lack of a coherent strategy between the Executive and Legislative branches on artificial intelligence.

YVQahJM3uq7nYorFkKZF.titulo: February 2026: Between AI-Powered Hackers and Broken Promises
YVQahJM3uq7nYorFkKZF.subtitulo: Mexico's government faces a month of contrasts: legislative progress even as it suffers its first documented AI-driven cyberattack
YVQahJM3uq7nYorFkKZF.contenido:
February 2026 marks a paradoxical moment for Mexico's government AI agenda. While the Senate approved the Ley General de Inteligencia Artificial (General Artificial Intelligence Law) in committee on February 12 — with a full-floor vote scheduled for February 25 — the country suffered its first documented mass cyberattack using generative AI.

A hacker used Claude, Anthropic's chatbot, to extract 150 gigabytes of government data between December and January, compromising records of 195 million SAT (tax authority) taxpayers, INE (electoral institute) credentials, and state government systems in Jalisco, Michoacan and Tamaulipas. The attack exposes the vulnerabilities of Mexico's digital infrastructure just as the country debates how to regulate this technology.

On the legislative front, the promise tracker shows mixed signals. Of 36 government announcements, 39% (14) are operational, while 42% (15) remain in development. The Centro Publico de Formacion en IA (Public AI Training Center) maintains its 10,000 active students, but a gap persists between the official figures reported and operational reality.

The federal government launched Impulsora de Innovación with 4 billion pesos to fund AI startups, signaling a shift toward public venture capital. Experts warn, however, that Mexico is debating regulation amid an institutional vacuum, following the disappearance of autonomous bodies such as INAI (transparency institute) and IFT (telecom regulator).

The education agenda showed concrete progress: AI-focused high school tracks were confirmed to be operating, with documented cases such as CBTIS 153 in Tlaxcala, while UAT (Universidad Autónoma de Tamaulipas) formalized its Instituto de IA (AI Institute).

PQYZfeIEZ2Ryw3qIhIu6.titulo: Silent January: AI governance on pause
PQYZfeIEZ2Ryw3qIhIu6.subtitulo: Zero progress on promises, legislation, and court cases in the year's first month
PQYZfeIEZ2Ryw3qIhIu6.contenido:
The first month of 2026 marks a notable contrast in Mexico's government AI agenda. While the Public AI Training Center (Lab-MexIA) began operations with its first cohort of 10,000 students as scheduled since November 2025, the government promise tracker shows a total absence of movement: 35 registered announcements with no status changes.

Of these 35 public commitments, only 37% (13) are effectively operating, while 40% (14) remain in development and 23% (8) are still at the promise stage. The government's compliance rate remains stalled at 2025 levels, with no documented progress in January.

On the legislative front, the 88 AI-related bills also recorded no movement. With only 5 approved historically (6%) against 59 rejected (67%), Congress maintains its pattern of inaction on technology regulation. The 6 existing court cases remain without updates.

The only relevant development was the Secretaría de Ciencia's (Science Ministry) announcement of the "Principios de Chapultepec" (Chapultepec Principles) on AI ethics, presented on January 29. These ten guiding principles seek to establish a responsible regulatory framework, though without immediate binding force.

Meanwhile, President Claudia Sheinbaum reiterated the need for a "national debate" on AI regulation to combat fraud, without settling on specific legislative initiatives.
